stem:
An 18-month-old boy who has just started walking is seen in a paediatric clinic because his ankles and knees have repeatedly become hot, swollen and too painful to bear weight, with no obvious injury. His mother's brother needed regular injections for a bleeding problem. His platelet count and PT are normal, but his APTT is prolonged.

Which inherited bleeding disorder is most likely?
why_correct: Haemophilia A is an X-linked deficiency of factor VIII, so it mainly affects boys and passes through carrier mothers, fitting an affected maternal uncle. Deep bleeding into joints and muscles is typical, often beginning when a child starts walking. A prolonged APTT with normal PT and platelets supports a factor VIII deficiency, confirmed by factor assay.
why_wrong: A. This is usually autosomal and causes mainly mucosal bleeding such as nosebleeds and heavy periods; joint bleeds are unusual except in the severe form. B. This is acquired, causes a low platelet count and gives petechiae and bruising rather than joint bleeds. C. This rare platelet function disorder causes mucocutaneous bleeding with a normal APTT. D. This causes nosebleeds and telangiectasia, not haemarthroses.
pearl: Haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) is clinically identical, so a factor assay is needed to tell them apart.
thinking: Boy with recurrent joint swelling ↓ Affected maternal uncle suggests X-linked inheritance ↓ Normal platelets and PT ↓ Prolonged APTT ↓ Factor VIII deficiency: haemophilia A
exam_trap: A, Von Willebrand disease — it is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder and can prolong the APTT, but it typically causes mucosal bleeding with autosomal inheritance.
takeaway: Recurrent haemarthroses in a boy with an affected maternal relative suggest haemophilia.

stem:
The parents of a 3-year-old boy newly diagnosed with severe haemophilia B ask the specialist nurse which kind of bleeding they should watch for most closely at home, compared with what they have read about platelet disorders.

Which bleeding pattern is most characteristic of his condition?

options.A: Pinpoint petechial rashes on the skin
options.E: Deep bleeding into joints and muscles

correct_answer: E. Deep bleeding into joints and muscles
why_correct: Haemophilia is a clotting factor deficiency, so platelet plug formation is normal but the clot cannot be stabilised. The result is delayed, deep bleeding into joints and muscles, with haemarthrosis the hallmark. Parents are taught to recognise early signs such as a child refusing to use a limb, warmth or swelling, so that factor replacement can be given quickly.
why_wrong: A. Petechiae suggest a low platelet count or platelet dysfunction. B. Mucosal bleeding is more typical of platelet disorders and von Willebrand disease. C. Bruising can occur, but superficial bleeding alone is not the characteristic pattern. D. Haematuria can occur but is not the defining bleeding pattern.
pearl: Recurrent bleeds into the same joint (a target joint) lead to chronic haemophilic arthropathy, which prophylactic factor replacement aims to prevent.
thinking: Clotting factor deficiency ↓ Platelet plug forms normally ↓ Clot cannot be stabilised ↓ Delayed deep bleeding ↓ Joints and muscles most affected
exam_trap: B, Recurrent nosebleeds and gum bleeding — these are common in bleeding disorders generally, but they point to platelet or von Willebrand problems rather than haemophilia.
takeaway: Haemophilia causes deep bleeding into joints and muscles; platelet disorders cause mucocutaneous bleeding.

presentation: Suspected deep vein thrombosis — low probability
stem:
After a coach journey across Europe, a 39-year-old woman calls into her GP practice with a mildly puffy left ankle and calf. She has no previous clots, takes no hormones and the calf is only slightly tender. Using the two-level Wells score, her GP judges DVT to be unlikely.

Which blood test is the appropriate next step?
why_correct: When the two-level Wells score says DVT is unlikely, NICE advises a D-dimer test. A negative result makes DVT very unlikely and allows an alternative diagnosis to be considered, while a positive result should lead to a proximal leg vein ultrasound. D-dimer has high sensitivity but low specificity, so it is useful only for ruling out.
why_wrong: B. CRP is a non-specific marker of inflammation and does not exclude a clot. C. Thrombophilia testing is not part of diagnosing an acute DVT and is rarely indicated. D. Troponin is for suspected myocardial injury. E. Creatine kinase reflects muscle damage and does not help exclude thrombosis.
pearl: D-dimer rises with age, pregnancy, infection, cancer and recent surgery, so a positive result in these settings is weak evidence of thrombosis.
thinking: Unilateral calf swelling after prolonged travel ↓ Wells score: DVT unlikely ↓ Need a rule-out test ↓ D-dimer ↓ Negative excludes, positive leads to ultrasound
exam_trap: C, Thrombophilia screen — it sounds relevant to clotting, but it does not diagnose an acute DVT and is not part of the initial pathway.
takeaway: In suspected DVT with a low Wells score, a negative D-dimer is used to rule thrombosis out.

stem:
A 74-year-old man is seen in the haematology clinic. Over several months he has noticed painless lumps in his right axilla and left groin, and examination also finds an enlarged node in the neck, with no involvement of the areas in between. He feels generally well.

Which diagnosis best explains this pattern of lymph node enlargement?
why_correct: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma often presents in older adults with painless lymphadenopathy in several separate, non-adjacent regions, because it spreads in a non-contiguous way. Hodgkin lymphoma, by contrast, typically spreads in an orderly fashion from one node group to the next. Diagnosis requires a lymph node biopsy.
why_wrong: A. Hodgkin lymphoma tends to spread to neighbouring node groups and is more often seen in young adults. B. Sarcoidosis classically causes bilateral hilar nodes rather than scattered peripheral nodes in an older man. C. Glandular fever affects young people and causes tender nodes with a sore throat. D. Tuberculosis usually involves a single region with constitutional symptoms.
pearl: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is far more common than Hodgkin lymphoma and its incidence rises steadily with age.
thinking: Older man ↓ Painless nodes ↓ Several separate, non-adjacent regions ↓ Non-contiguous spread ↓ Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
exam_trap: A, Hodgkin lymphoma — lymphoma is clearly suspected, but skipping between distant node groups and older age favour non-Hodgkin disease.
takeaway: Painless lymphadenopathy in non-adjacent regions in an older adult suggests non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman had an enlarged axillary node removed after it persisted for three months. The histopathology report confirms classical Hodgkin lymphoma, with the malignant cells staining positive for CD15 and CD30.

Which cell type is the characteristic finding that supports this diagnosis?
why_correct: Reed-Sternberg cells are large, often binucleate cells with prominent nucleoli, giving an owl's eye appearance, and are the hallmark of classical Hodgkin lymphoma. They are typically CD15 and CD30 positive. They make up a small proportion of the tumour, surrounded by a reactive inflammatory background.
why_wrong: A. Smudge cells are seen on the blood film in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. B. Atypical lymphocytes are typical of glandular fever. D. Plasma cells are the malignant cells in myeloma. E. Myeloid blasts indicate acute myeloid leukaemia.
pearl: Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma in the UK.
thinking: Persistent enlarged node ↓ Excision biopsy ↓ Classical Hodgkin lymphoma with CD15 and CD30 positivity ↓ Large binucleate owl's eye cells ↓ Reed-Sternberg cells
exam_trap: B, Atypical reactive lymphocytes — they are also linked with enlarged nodes in young adults, but they indicate glandular fever, not lymphoma.
takeaway: The Reed-Sternberg cell is the characteristic cell of classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

stem:
A 38-year-old man is being staged for newly diagnosed lymphoma. During the clinic review he lists the symptoms he has noticed over recent months: itchy skin, tiredness, aching in his neck lump after drinking beer, a dry cough and waking with his sheets soaked in sweat.

Which of these is classed as a B symptom for staging?

options.B: Pain in the node after alcohol

why_correct: B symptoms are unexplained fever above 38°C, drenching night sweats and unintentional loss of more than 10% of body weight within six months. They are recorded in staging because they indicate more active disease and influence prognosis and treatment. Night sweats that soak the bedding meet this definition.
why_wrong: A. Pruritus is common in Hodgkin lymphoma but is not counted as a B symptom. B. Alcohol-induced node pain is a classic feature of Hodgkin disease but not a B symptom. C. Fatigue is common but non-specific and not part of the definition. D. Cough may reflect mediastinal disease but is not a B symptom.
pearl: The letter B is added to the stage (for example stage IIB) when any of the three B symptoms is present.
thinking: Lymphoma staging ↓ B symptoms: fever, night sweats, weight loss ↓ Check each symptom against the definition ↓ Soaked sheets at night qualifies ↓ Drenching night sweats
exam_trap: A, Generalised itching — it is a well-known lymphoma symptom, but it is not one of the three formal B symptoms.
takeaway: The B symptoms of lymphoma are fever, drenching night sweats and significant unexplained weight loss.

stem:
A 44-year-old woman asks her practice nurse whether a lump under her jaw could be serious. The nurse arranges for her to see the GP, who considers which feature of a lymph node would most raise concern about cancer.

Which finding is the most worrying?

options.A: A tender node that appeared during a head cold
options.B: A soft, mobile node smaller than a pea
options.C: A painless node that has kept growing for over two months
options.D: A node that has shrunk steadily over two weeks
options.E: A tender node next to a recent dental abscess

correct_answer: C. A painless node that has kept growing for over two months
why_correct: Painless, persistent and progressive enlargement suggests a node is not reacting to infection but is infiltrated by malignancy such as lymphoma or metastatic cancer. Reactive nodes are usually tender, appear with an obvious infection and shrink within a few weeks. A node that keeps growing for more than a few weeks warrants urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Tender nodes during a viral illness are usually reactive. B. Small, soft, mobile nodes are typically benign. D. A shrinking node is resolving and reassuring. E. A tender node near a dental abscess is explained by local infection.
pearl: Tenderness usually suggests inflammation, whereas cancer often causes painless nodes, although rapidly growing lymphoma can occasionally be tender.
thinking: Neck lump in an adult ↓ Reactive nodes: tender, with infection, resolve ↓ Malignant nodes: painless, persistent, progressive ↓ Compare each option ↓ Painless growing node is most concerning
exam_trap: E, A tender node next to a recent dental abscess — a node can seem alarming because of the pain, but tenderness with a local infection points to a reactive cause.
takeaway: A painless lymph node that keeps enlarging over weeks is a red flag for malignancy.

stem:
A 69-year-old man who smokes returns to his GP. Six weeks ago he had a cough and sore throat and was given antibiotics, and although those symptoms settled, two firm painless nodes below his right ear have not changed. He has no fever and no dental or skin infection.

Which is the most likely cause that must be excluded?

options.B: Reactive lymphadenopathy after a viral infection

why_correct: Firm, painless nodes that persist for weeks after an infection has resolved, in an older smoker, should raise concern about malignancy, such as metastatic head and neck cancer or lymphoma. Reactive nodes should settle once the trigger has gone. He needs urgent referral for examination of the upper aerodigestive tract and tissue sampling.
why_wrong: B. Reactive nodes usually shrink within a few weeks of the infection resolving. C. A branchial cyst usually presents in younger adults as a smooth fluctuant swelling. D. A salivary stone causes swelling and pain linked to eating. E. A thyroglossal cyst is a midline lump that moves with tongue protrusion.
pearl: Persistent neck lumps in older smokers or heavy drinkers should prompt a search for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
thinking: Older smoker ↓ Firm painless nodes in the neck ↓ Persist after infection has settled ↓ Not a reactive pattern ↓ Exclude malignancy
exam_trap: B, Reactive lymphadenopathy after a viral infection — the recent illness offers an easy explanation, but reactive nodes should resolve, not persist unchanged for six weeks.
takeaway: Neck nodes that persist after an infection settles, especially in an older smoker, must be investigated for cancer.

stem:
A 52-year-old man with long-standing alcohol excess is found to have a macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils on the blood film. Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels have been sent.

Which statement about a low folate, as opposed to a low cobalamin, is true?

options.A: Folate deficiency produces a microcytic blood film
options.B: Folate deficiency raises serum methylmalonic acid
options.C: Folate deficiency rarely causes neurological damage
options.D: Folate deficiency causes a marked rise in platelet count
options.E: Folate deficiency does not cause megaloblastic change

correct_answer: C. Folate deficiency rarely causes neurological damage
why_correct: Both deficiencies cause a megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia, but neurological complications such as peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord are features of B12 deficiency. Folate deficiency rarely causes these problems. This is why B12 should be checked and replaced before or alongside folic acid, as folic acid alone can worsen neurological damage in B12 deficiency.
why_wrong: A. Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis, not microcytosis. B. Raised methylmalonic acid is a marker of B12 deficiency and is normal in folate deficiency. D. Thrombocytosis is not a feature, and platelets may fall. E. Folate deficiency does cause megaloblastic change.
pearl: Homocysteine is raised in both folate and B12 deficiency, whereas methylmalonic acid is raised only in B12 deficiency.
thinking: Macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils ↓ Megaloblastic picture ↓ Folate or B12 deficiency ↓ Neurological damage is a B12 feature ↓ Folate deficiency rarely affects nerves
exam_trap: B, Folate deficiency raises serum methylmalonic acid — it is a true distinguishing test, but it is raised in B12 deficiency, not folate deficiency.
takeaway: Neurological complications point to vitamin B12 rather than folate deficiency.
notes: Reviewer fix: Stem: replaced awkward sentence about the registrar reviewing how each vitamin behaves with 'Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels have been sent.'

stem:
A 67-year-old man is referred to the renal clinic with marked ankle oedema and heavy proteinuria. He also reports breathlessness on exertion, and an echocardiogram shows thickened ventricular walls with a restrictive filling pattern. He has burning, numb feet and carpal tunnel symptoms in both hands, and his tongue looks enlarged. His HbA1c is normal.

Which systemic condition best explains these findings?
why_correct: Amyloidosis causes extracellular deposition of misfolded protein in many organs, giving nephrotic syndrome, restrictive cardiomyopathy with thick walls and peripheral and autonomic neuropathy. Macroglossia and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome are classic clues, particularly in AL amyloidosis linked to a plasma cell disorder. Diagnosis is by tissue biopsy with Congo red staining.
why_wrong: A. Hypothyroidism can cause carpal tunnel and an enlarged tongue but not nephrotic-range proteinuria. B. Sarcoidosis can affect the heart and nerves but rarely causes nephrotic syndrome or macroglossia. C. Multiple sclerosis affects the central nervous system only. D. Haemochromatosis causes cardiomyopathy, diabetes and liver disease but not heavy proteinuria.
pearl: Amyloid on biopsy shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light after Congo red staining.
thinking: Nephrotic syndrome without diabetes ↓ Thick-walled restrictive heart ↓ Peripheral neuropathy and carpal tunnel ↓ Macroglossia ↓ Multisystem amyloid deposition
exam_trap: A, Hypothyroidism — it explains the large tongue and carpal tunnel, but not heavy proteinuria and restrictive cardiomyopathy.
takeaway: Nephrotic syndrome, restrictive cardiomyopathy and neuropathy together suggest amyloidosis.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman attends her GP surgery after her partner noticed swellings on the side of her neck. She describes drenching sweats that soak the bedsheets and has felt worn out for two months. The GP is weighing up reactive lymphadenopathy against something more sinister.

Which feature in her history or examination most strongly points towards lymphoma?

options.A: A single tender node that appeared during a recent tooth abscess
options.B: Rubbery, non-tender nodes that have persisted for weeks alongside drenching night sweats
options.C: A blocked nose and sneezing for the past week
options.D: Sore, enlarged nodes that came on with a throat infection three days ago
options.E: A scratchy throat that settled within a day

correct_answer: B. Rubbery, non-tender nodes that have persisted for weeks alongside drenching night sweats
why_correct: Lymphoma typically produces painless, rubbery nodes that persist rather than settling after an infection. When this is combined with B symptoms such as drenching night sweats, the picture is far more suggestive of lymphoma than of a reactive process. This combination warrants urgent investigation, including blood tests and referral for node assessment or biopsy.
why_wrong: A. A tender node linked to a dental infection is typically reactive and settles with the infection. C. Nasal congestion is a non-specific upper respiratory symptom. D. Tender nodes appearing with an acute throat infection are an expected reactive response. E. A brief scratchy throat is non-specific and self-limiting.
pearl: B symptoms of lymphoma are fever, drenching night sweats and unexplained weight loss; their presence affects staging and prognosis.
thinking: Neck swellings with night sweats and fatigue ↓ Reactive nodes are tender, linked to infection and resolve ↓ Malignant nodes are painless, rubbery and persistent ↓ Systemic B symptoms add weight ↓ Persistent painless nodes plus night sweats favour lymphoma
exam_trap: D, Sore nodes with a throat infection — enlarged nodes sound worrying, but tenderness and a clear infective trigger point to a reactive cause rather than lymphoma.
takeaway: Persistent painless lymphadenopathy with B symptoms should raise suspicion of lymphoma.

stem:
On a surgical ward, a staff nurse is about to hang a unit of red cells for an 82-year-old man who became anaemic after a hip fracture repair. The bag has been collected from the blood fridge and the prescription is signed.

Before connecting the unit, which step is essential to prevent the most dangerous type of transfusion error?

options.A: Warm the bag to body temperature in a bowl of hot water
options.B: Give intravenous chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone as routine premedication
options.C: Check the patient's identity at the bedside against the blood component label and the prescription
options.D: Send a fresh group and save sample before starting
options.E: Make sure he has had nothing to eat for six hours

correct_answer: C. Check the patient's identity at the bedside against the blood component label and the prescription
why_correct: The most serious transfusion hazard is giving the wrong blood to the wrong patient, which can cause ABO-incompatible haemolysis and death. A final bedside check, matching the patient's identity details (ideally stated by the patient and confirmed on the wristband) with the component label and the prescription, is the last barrier against this error. It must be done at the bedside immediately before the unit is connected.
why_wrong: A. Components should not be warmed in improvised hot water; a validated blood warmer is used only in specific situations such as rapid transfusion. B. Routine premedication is not recommended and may mask a reaction. D. A valid sample was used for crossmatching already; a new sample does not replace the bedside check. E. Fasting is not required for a blood transfusion.
pearl: Wrong blood in tube and wrong component transfused incidents are reported to SHOT, the UK haemovigilance scheme; most ABO-incompatible transfusions result from a missed or rushed bedside identity check.
thinking: Unit ready to be given ↓ Biggest risk is wrong blood to wrong patient ↓ ABO incompatibility can be fatal ↓ Final barrier is positive patient identification ↓ Check patient ID against the component and prescription at the bedside
exam_trap: D, Sending a fresh group and save sample — it sounds thorough, but compatibility testing has already been done and only a bedside identity check catches a wrong-patient error.
takeaway: Always perform a bedside identity check of patient against blood component immediately before transfusion.
notes: Reviewer fix: pearl reworded: removed reliance on the NHS never-events classification (framework under revision); now states SHOT reporting and bedside-check failure as the usual cause

stem:
A 63-year-old man with a ruddy, plethoric face is reviewed in clinic. Repeated tests over a year show erythrocytosis with a high packed cell volume, and JAK2 testing is awaited. He wonders whether any of his recent complaints relate to sluggish flow of his thickened blood.

Which complaint is best explained by this?

options.A: Bleeding into the knee joint after minor knocks
options.B: Yellowing of the skin and eyes
options.C: Passing large volumes of dilute urine with constant thirst
options.E: Headaches with a feeling of fullness in the head

correct_answer: E. Headaches with a feeling of fullness in the head
why_correct: A raised red cell mass increases blood viscosity and slows flow through small vessels, particularly in the brain. This commonly causes headache, a sense of fullness, dizziness, tinnitus and visual disturbance. His persistent erythrocytosis and plethora fit this mechanism.
why_wrong: A. Haemarthrosis is a feature of clotting factor deficiencies such as haemophilia. B. Jaundice suggests haemolysis or liver disease, not hyperviscosity. C. Polyuria with thirst points to diabetes insipidus or diabetes mellitus. D. Diarrhoea is not a recognised effect of a raised haematocrit.
pearl: In polycythaemia vera, venesection to keep the haematocrit below a target level reduces the risk of thrombosis; itching after a warm bath (aquagenic pruritus) is a classic additional symptom.
thinking: Persistently raised haemoglobin and haematocrit ↓ Increased red cell mass ↓ Raised blood viscosity and sluggish cerebral flow ↓ Headache, fullness, dizziness and visual blurring ↓ Headache is the viscosity-related symptom
exam_trap: A, Bleeding into a joint — polycythaemia vera can cause bleeding, which makes this tempting, but haemarthrosis is the hallmark of factor deficiencies, not hyperviscosity.
takeaway: A raised red cell mass thickens the blood and typically causes headache and other hyperviscosity symptoms.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman has a high platelet count found on bloods taken at her blood pressure review. Repeat counts over the next three months remain persistently raised. Her ferritin, inflammatory markers and examination are normal, and she has had no recent surgery, infection or bleeding.

Which diagnosis should now be considered?
why_correct: Most raised platelet counts are reactive, due to iron deficiency, infection, inflammation, bleeding or malignancy. Here those causes have been excluded and the thrombocytosis is persistent. That makes a primary myeloproliferative neoplasm, essential thrombocythaemia, the condition to consider, and she should be referred to haematology for further testing.
why_wrong: A. Aplastic anaemia causes low counts across all cell lines, not a high platelet count. B. Immune thrombocytopenia causes a low platelet count. D. Iron deficiency can cause reactive thrombocytosis, but her ferritin is normal. E. Haemophilia A is a clotting factor deficiency with a normal platelet count.
pearl: About half of patients with essential thrombocythaemia carry the JAK2 V617F mutation; most of the rest have CALR or MPL mutations.
thinking: Persistently high platelets ↓ Look for reactive causes first ↓ Normal ferritin, inflammatory markers and no bleeding or infection ↓ Primary marrow overproduction likely ↓ Essential thrombocythaemia
exam_trap: D, Iron-deficiency anaemia — iron deficiency is a common cause of a raised platelet count, but her normal ferritin excludes it here.
takeaway: Persistent unexplained thrombocytosis without a reactive cause suggests essential thrombocythaemia.

stem:
A 68-year-old man was diagnosed with essential thrombocythaemia last year but has stopped his medication and missed his haematology follow-up. His GP reviews him and wants to explain why ongoing treatment matters.

Which complication is he at greatest risk of if the condition remains untreated?
why_correct: Essential thrombocythaemia is a myeloproliferative neoplasm in which a high number of often dysfunctional platelets predisposes to arterial and venous thrombosis, such as stroke, myocardial infarction and deep vein thrombosis. Older age and previous thrombosis increase this risk further, which is why he would usually be treated. Bleeding can also occur, especially at very high counts, but thrombosis is the main concern.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary fibrosis is not a feature of essential thrombocythaemia. B. Diabetes insipidus has no link to a raised platelet count. C. Cataracts are unrelated. E. Hypocalcaemia is not caused by thrombocytosis.
pearl: Higher-risk patients with essential thrombocythaemia are usually offered low-dose aspirin plus cytoreduction, most often with hydroxycarbamide.
thinking: Known essential thrombocythaemia ↓ Untreated and older ↓ High numbers of abnormal platelets ↓ Increased arterial and venous clotting ↓ Thrombosis is the key risk
exam_trap: E, Profound hypocalcaemia — haematological malignancy brings electrolyte problems to mind, but calcium disturbance is a feature of myeloma, not essential thrombocythaemia.
takeaway: Thrombosis is the main complication of essential thrombocythaemia, so high-risk patients need treatment.

stem:
Bloods taken at a pre-operative assessment before a 39-year-old man's hernia repair show a markedly raised white-cell count. He feels well apart from mild tiredness. The haematology laboratory phones the clinic because the film shows a striking excess of basophils.

Which condition is most likely?

options.A: Reactive leucocytosis due to bacterial infection

why_correct: A very high white-cell count with prominent basophilia is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukaemia, a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene. CML is often found incidentally on a routine blood count in the chronic phase. Reactive causes do not usually produce marked basophilia, so this finding should prompt urgent haematology referral.
why_wrong: A. Bacterial infection raises the neutrophil count, sometimes with a left shift, but not marked basophilia, and he is well. B. Myeloma is a plasma cell disorder and does not cause a high white-cell count with basophilia. D. Immune thrombocytopenia causes isolated low platelets. E. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia causes a lymphocytosis with smear cells, not basophilia.
pearl: The Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), produces the BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase, which is targeted by tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.
thinking: Incidental high white-cell count ↓ Film shows marked basophilia ↓ Basophilia is unusual in reactive states ↓ Suggests a myeloproliferative process ↓ Chronic myeloid leukaemia
exam_trap: E, Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia — it is also found incidentally in well adults with a high white-cell count, but it shows mature lymphocytes rather than basophils.
takeaway: Marked leucocytosis with basophilia should raise suspicion of chronic myeloid leukaemia.

stem:
A 30-year-old man having chemotherapy for testicular cancer is warned by the oncology nurse that his treatment suppresses the marrow, so he must look out for fever. He asks which part of his immune system engulfs and kills bacteria in the first hours of an infection.

Which cell is responsible?
why_correct: Neutrophils are the most numerous white cells and the main phagocytes of innate immunity. They migrate rapidly to sites of infection and engulf and kill bacteria and fungi. Chemotherapy commonly suppresses them, which is why neutropenia carries a high risk of serious bacterial infection.
why_wrong: B. Eosinophils mainly defend against parasites and take part in allergic responses. C. Erythrocytes carry oxygen and have no role in killing bacteria. D. Platelets are involved in haemostasis. E. Basophils release histamine in allergic and inflammatory reactions.
pearl: The neutrophil nadir after most cytotoxic chemotherapy typically occurs about 7 to 14 days after treatment, when infection risk is highest.
thinking: Chemotherapy lowers the white-cell count ↓ Question asks about defence against bacteria ↓ Innate phagocytes act first ↓ Neutrophils engulf and kill bacteria ↓ Neutrophils are the key cell
exam_trap: B, Eosinophils — they are white cells involved in immunity, but their main role is against parasites and in allergy rather than bacterial infection.
takeaway: Neutrophils are the main defence against bacterial infection, so neutropenia greatly increases infection risk.

stem:
A 74-year-old woman with multiple myeloma has needed three courses of antibiotics this winter for chest infections, one of them pneumococcal. Her daughter asks the haematology specialist nurse why she keeps getting unwell.

Which mechanism chiefly explains her susceptibility to bacterial infection?

options.A: Reduced production of normal, functioning antibodies
options.B: Overproduction of red cells crowding the marrow
options.E: Thickened blood preventing white cells reaching tissues

correct_answer: A. Reduced production of normal, functioning antibodies
why_correct: In myeloma, a single clone of plasma cells expands and produces a paraprotein while normal polyclonal immunoglobulin production falls (immunoparesis). Low levels of functional antibody leave her particularly vulnerable to encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. Treatment-related neutropenia and steroids can add to the risk, but antibody deficiency is the central problem.
why_wrong: B. Myeloma reduces normal red cell production, causing anaemia. C. Myeloma does not increase platelet production. D. Hypercalcaemia does not directly destroy neutrophils. E. Hyperviscosity can occur but is not the main reason for recurrent bacterial infection.
pearl: Patients with myeloma who have recurrent infections and low immunoglobulin levels may be offered immunoglobulin replacement, and pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccines are recommended.
thinking: Myeloma with repeated chest infections ↓ Clonal plasma cells make a single paraprotein ↓ Normal polyclonal antibody production is suppressed ↓ Poor defence against encapsulated bacteria ↓ Immunoparesis explains the infections
exam_trap: E, Thickened blood — myeloma can cause hyperviscosity, so this sounds plausible, but recurrent bacterial infections are explained by loss of normal antibody production.
takeaway: Recurrent bacterial infections in myeloma are mainly due to suppressed normal immunoglobulin production.

stem:
A 27-year-old man phones the acute oncology helpline eight days after his second cycle of chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. He was warned that his neutrophil count would drop after each cycle. During the call he mentions several symptoms.

Which one should prompt immediate hospital assessment for neutropenic sepsis?

options.A: A tension-type headache with no other symptoms
options.B: Feeling hot and shivery with a raised temperature
options.D: Patchy dry skin on his elbows
options.E: Sneezing from his usual hay fever

correct_answer: B. Feeling hot and shivery with a raised temperature
why_correct: He is in the expected neutrophil nadir after chemotherapy, so fever or rigors may be the only sign of overwhelming infection. Neutropenic sepsis is a medical emergency, and he needs urgent assessment and empirical intravenous antibiotics without waiting for a blood count. The other symptoms are common and benign.
why_wrong: A. An isolated headache without fever or other features does not suggest neutropenic sepsis. C. Constipation is a common side effect of antiemetics such as ondansetron. D. Dry skin is not a sign of systemic infection. E. Ongoing hay fever symptoms are not concerning.
pearl: NICE advises that empirical antibiotics for suspected neutropenic sepsis are given immediately, within 1 hour of arrival, with piperacillin with tazobactam as the usual first-line choice.
thinking: Recent chemotherapy ↓ Expected neutrophil nadir ↓ Inflammatory signs of infection may be absent ↓ Fever or rigors may be the only clue ↓ Treat as neutropenic sepsis urgently
exam_trap: A, Headache — new symptoms during chemotherapy can feel alarming, but a headache without fever or other features is not a marker of neutropenic sepsis.
takeaway: In a neutropenic patient, fever or rigors mean neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise.

stem:
An 81-year-old woman in a care home has become increasingly tired and has needed antibiotics twice in the past month. Her blood tests show a very low neutrophil count, while her haemoglobin and platelets are normal. Her GP is reviewing a recently started medicine that may be responsible.

Which complication is she most at risk of because of this result?
why_correct: Neutrophils are the main defence against bacteria and fungi, so a very low count leaves her prone to rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection. Her recent infections fit this pattern. Signs of infection may be muted, so any fever or deterioration needs urgent assessment, and the likely causative drug should be reviewed.
why_wrong: A. Spontaneous bleeding is a risk of thrombocytopenia, and her platelets are normal. B. Tumour lysis syndrome follows treatment of bulky or rapidly dividing cancers, not isolated neutropenia. C. Hyperviscosity results from high cell counts or paraproteins, not low neutrophils. E. Autoimmune haemolysis causes anaemia and is unrelated to neutropenia.
pearl: Drugs commonly causing neutropenia or agranulocytosis include carbimazole, clozapine and sulfasalazine; patients on carbimazole are told to report a sore throat or fever promptly.
thinking: Very low neutrophils with normal other counts ↓ Recurrent infections already ↓ Neutrophils kill bacteria and fungi ↓ Defence against infection is impaired ↓ Risk of severe bacterial infection
exam_trap: A, Spontaneous bleeding from the gums — it is a classic complication of marrow problems, but bleeding reflects low platelets, which are normal here.
takeaway: Severe neutropenia puts patients at high risk of serious bacterial infection.

stem:
A 69-year-old man was diagnosed with multiple myeloma three months ago. At his clinic review his creatinine has risen considerably from baseline. He takes no NSAIDs, is well hydrated, and his urine contains large amounts of free kappa light chains.

Which process is most likely to be damaging his kidneys?

options.A: Cast nephropathy caused by filtered monoclonal light chains
options.B: IgA deposition in the glomerular mesangium
options.C: Narrowing of the renal arteries by atheroma
options.D: Podocyte foot-process effacement of minimal change disease

correct_answer: A. Cast nephropathy caused by filtered monoclonal light chains
why_correct: Free monoclonal light chains are filtered by the glomerulus and combine with Tamm-Horsfall protein in the distal tubule to form obstructing casts. They are also directly toxic to proximal tubular cells. This light-chain cast nephropathy (myeloma kidney) is the commonest cause of renal impairment in myeloma, and his heavy light-chain excretion supports it.
why_wrong: B. IgA nephropathy is a primary glomerulonephritis usually presenting with haematuria, not a myeloma complication. C. Renal artery stenosis is a vascular disease unrelated to light chains. D. Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome and is not typical of myeloma. E. Polycystic kidney disease is inherited and would not appear after a myeloma diagnosis.
pearl: Other contributors to renal impairment in myeloma include hypercalcaemia, dehydration, NSAIDs and amyloidosis; nephrotoxic drugs and contrast should be avoided where possible.
thinking: Myeloma with rising creatinine ↓ Large amounts of free light chains in urine ↓ Light chains filtered and precipitate in tubules ↓ Tubular obstruction and direct toxicity ↓ Light-chain cast nephropathy
exam_trap: D, Minimal change disease — myeloma kidneys can leak protein, which makes a glomerular cause tempting, but light-chain casts are the typical mechanism of renal injury.
takeaway: Light-chain cast nephropathy is the main cause of kidney injury in multiple myeloma.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman has back pain, a raised calcium and a rising creatinine. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a single narrow band in the gamma region, and a bone marrow biopsy confirms a clonal population of plasma cells. Her son asks what the abnormal band represents.

Which protein do the malignant cells produce?

options.A: Polyclonal immunoglobulin from many plasma cell lines
options.C: A monoclonal immunoglobulin (paraprotein) or its free light chains

correct_answer: C. A monoclonal immunoglobulin (paraprotein) or its free light chains
why_correct: Myeloma arises from a single clone of plasma cells, so they all secrete an identical immunoglobulin, seen as a narrow spike (M band) on electrophoresis. Some myelomas secrete only free light chains. These proteins can damage the kidneys, which fits her rising creatinine.
why_wrong: A. Polyclonal immunoglobulin produces a broad increase across the gamma region, as in chronic inflammation, not a narrow band. B. Fibrinogen is made by the liver. D. Haemoglobin is produced within developing red cells. E. Albumin is synthesised by the liver and is not produced by plasma cells.
pearl: When myeloma is suspected, serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and a serum free light chain assay are used together to detect a paraprotein.
thinking: Bone pain, high calcium and renal impairment ↓ Narrow band on electrophoresis ↓ Clonal plasma cells in the marrow ↓ A single clone makes one identical immunoglobulin ↓ Monoclonal paraprotein or light chains
exam_trap: A, Polyclonal immunoglobulin — plasma cells do make immunoglobulin, but a single malignant clone makes one monoclonal protein, not a polyclonal mix.
takeaway: Myeloma plasma cells secrete a monoclonal immunoglobulin or free light chains, seen as an M band.

stem:
An 18-year-old man with sickle cell disease comes to the emergency department after a cold night camping, complaining of intense pain in his lower back and both thighs. He has no chest symptoms, his spleen is not palpable and his haemoglobin and reticulocyte count are similar to his previous results.

Which is the most likely explanation for his pain?
why_correct: Cold exposure is a recognised trigger for sickling, and sickled cells obstruct small vessels in bone marrow, causing ischaemic bone pain in the back and limbs. His haemoglobin is at baseline and there is no splenomegaly, which makes complications causing a fall in haemoglobin unlikely. This is the commonest acute presentation of sickle cell disease.
why_wrong: A. Splenic sequestration causes an enlarging spleen and a sharp fall in haemoglobin, mainly in young children. B. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain, not back and thigh pain. C. Aplastic crisis causes a sudden drop in haemoglobin with a very low reticulocyte count. E. Hyperhaemolysis causes a fall in haemoglobin, often after transfusion.
pearl: NICE advises giving analgesia within 30 minutes of arrival for an acute painful sickle cell episode, using a strong opioid for severe pain and avoiding pethidine.
thinking: Known sickle cell disease ↓ Cold exposure trigger ↓ Severe back and limb pain ↓ Haemoglobin and reticulocytes at baseline, no splenomegaly ↓ Vaso-occlusive crisis
exam_trap: C, Parvovirus-induced aplastic crisis — it is a classic sickle complication, but it presents with a sudden fall in haemoglobin and low reticulocytes, not bone pain with stable counts.
takeaway: Severe bone pain with stable blood counts in sickle cell disease suggests a vaso-occlusive crisis.

stem:
A 57-year-old woman sees her GP with three months of tiredness and a dragging sensation under her left ribs; she now feels full after small meals. Her spleen is palpable well below the costal margin. A blood count shows a very high white-cell count, and the film reports myelocytes, metamyelocytes and neutrophils at every stage of maturation.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Massive splenomegaly causing early satiety and left upper quadrant discomfort, combined with a very high white-cell count showing granulocytes at all stages of maturation, is the classic chronic-phase picture of CML. The film reflects uncontrolled proliferation of the myeloid line. The diagnosis is confirmed by finding the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene.
why_wrong: B. CLL causes a lymphocytosis of mature small lymphocytes, not a spectrum of granulocyte precursors. C. Immune thrombocytopenia causes isolated low platelets without splenomegaly. D. Iron deficiency causes a microcytic anaemia, not a very high white-cell count. E. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolysis with spherocytes, not leucocytosis.
pearl: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib have transformed CML, giving most patients in the chronic phase a near-normal life expectancy.
thinking: Tiredness, left upper quadrant dragging and early satiety ↓ Large spleen on examination ↓ Very high white-cell count ↓ Granulocytes at every maturation stage ↓ Chronic myeloid leukaemia
exam_trap: B, Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia — it also causes a high white-cell count and can enlarge the spleen, but the cells are mature lymphocytes rather than myeloid precursors.
takeaway: Massive splenomegaly with a very high white-cell count across all granulocyte stages suggests CML.

presentation: Suspected DVT when ultrasound is delayed
stem:
A 46-year-old woman attends an urgent treatment centre late on a Friday evening with a swollen, tender left calf that developed after a long-haul flight. Using the two-level Wells score, DVT is likely. The radiology department confirms that no venous ultrasound will be available until the next morning. She has no contraindication to anticoagulation.

How should she be managed?

options.A: Request a CT pulmonary angiogram instead of the leg ultrasound
options.B: Take a D-dimer, start interim therapeutic anticoagulation and arrange the ultrasound within 24 hours
options.C: Give prophylactic-dose LMWH and book an ultrasound within 72 hours
options.D: Start aspirin and arrange the ultrasound within 24 hours
options.E: Discharge without treatment and book an outpatient scan within a week

correct_answer: B. Take a D-dimer, start interim therapeutic anticoagulation and arrange the ultrasound within 24 hours
why_correct: NICE NG158 advises that when DVT is likely and a proximal leg-vein ultrasound cannot be performed within 4 hours, a D-dimer test should be taken and interim therapeutic anticoagulation started. The ultrasound should then be done within 24 hours. This protects her from clot propagation and embolism while she waits for imaging.
why_wrong: A. A CT pulmonary angiogram investigates pulmonary embolism and cannot diagnose a leg DVT. C. Prophylactic-dose LMWH is inadequate for a suspected DVT, and a 72-hour delay is too long. D. Aspirin is not an effective treatment for venous thromboembolism. E. Leaving a likely DVT untreated for a week risks pulmonary embolism.
pearl: Apixaban or rivaroxaban are suitable interim anticoagulants because they can be continued if DVT is confirmed.
thinking: Wells score: DVT likely ↓ Ultrasound not possible within 4 hours ↓ Take a D-dimer ↓ Start interim therapeutic anticoagulation ↓ Scan within 24 hours
exam_trap: C, Prophylactic-dose LMWH with a later scan — giving some heparin feels like a safe compromise, but only a therapeutic dose protects against propagation of a suspected DVT.
takeaway: If DVT is likely and ultrasound is delayed, start interim therapeutic anticoagulation after a D-dimer and scan within 24 hours.

stem:
A 58-year-old man attends the ambulatory care unit with three days of a painful, swollen left calf after a long-haul flight. His two-level Wells score puts DVT in the likely category, and interim apixaban was started. A proximal leg vein Doppler performed this morning shows no thrombus.

What is the most appropriate next investigation?
why_correct: When DVT is likely on the two-level Wells score and the proximal ultrasound is negative, NICE NG158 advises a D-dimer test. A negative D-dimer allows interim anticoagulation to stop and DVT to be excluded. A positive D-dimer means a repeat proximal ultrasound about a week later, with interim anticoagulation stopped meanwhile.
why_wrong: B. CTPA investigates pulmonary embolism and he has no chest symptoms. C. Venography is invasive and is not part of the standard NICE pathway. D. Thrombophilia testing does not diagnose an acute clot and is not routine. E. A repeat scan, when needed, is done within about a week after a positive D-dimer, not months later.
pearl: In the NICE DVT pathway, a positive D-dimer after a negative scan leads to a repeat proximal ultrasound 6 to 8 days later rather than immediate further imaging.
thinking: Likely Wells score ↓ First proximal ultrasound negative ↓ Pathway is not complete ↓ D-dimer decides next step ↓ Negative excludes DVT; positive means repeat scan in about a week
exam_trap: E, Repeat proximal Doppler in 3 months — repeating the scan is part of the pathway, which makes it tempting, but it follows a positive D-dimer and is done within days, not months.
takeaway: A negative proximal scan with a likely Wells score should be followed by a D-dimer.

stem:
On a Friday evening, a 46-year-old woman is seen in the emergency department with a hot, tender, swollen right leg. She had a hysterectomy two weeks ago and her Wells score makes DVT likely. The vascular sonographer has gone home and the earliest scan available is tomorrow morning. She has no bleeding risk factors.

What is the most appropriate management now?

options.B: Discharge with a routine outpatient scan next week
options.C: Start a therapeutic-dose anticoagulant and scan within 24 hours
options.E: Withhold anticoagulation until the clot is confirmed

correct_answer: C. Start a therapeutic-dose anticoagulant and scan within 24 hours
why_correct: NICE NG158 advises that if a proximal leg vein ultrasound cannot be done within 4 hours for a person with a likely Wells score, interim therapeutic anticoagulation should be offered and the scan carried out within 24 hours. A DOAC such as apixaban or rivaroxaban is preferred because it can be continued if DVT is confirmed. Her recent major surgery gives a high pre-test probability, so delay without cover is unsafe.
why_wrong: A. Aspirin does not treat venous thrombosis. B. The scan must be done within 24 hours, not next week. D. Prophylactic doses are inadequate for a suspected established clot. E. Leaving a likely DVT untreated risks pulmonary embolism while waiting.
pearl: Apixaban or rivaroxaban is the preferred interim anticoagulant because it can simply continue as treatment if the scan confirms DVT.
thinking: Wells score likely ↓ Scan not available within 4 hours ↓ No contraindication to anticoagulation ↓ Start interim therapeutic dose ↓ Ultrasound within 24 hours
exam_trap: D, Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin until the scan — it feels like a cautious middle ground, but a suspected clot needs a treatment dose, not a prevention dose.
takeaway: If a likely DVT cannot be scanned within 4 hours, give interim therapeutic anticoagulation and scan within 24 hours.

stem:
A surgical foundation doctor is completing VTE risk assessments for five people on an orthopaedic and day-case list.

Which person has a recognised risk factor that increases their chance of developing a venous thromboembolism?

options.B: A 30-year-old woman who wears glasses for short-sightedness
options.C: A 67-year-old man confined to bed after a hip replacement
options.D: A 35-year-old woman who walks 5 km daily
options.E: A 40-year-old man with a healed graze on his knee

correct_answer: C. A 67-year-old man confined to bed after a hip replacement
why_correct: Major orthopaedic surgery such as hip replacement combined with reduced mobility is one of the strongest risk factors for VTE. Surgery causes endothelial injury and a hypercoagulable state, and immobility adds venous stasis, completing Virchow's triad. NICE NG89 advises risk assessment and thromboprophylaxis for such patients.
why_wrong: A. Hay fever does not increase thrombotic risk. B. Myopia has no link to VTE. D. Regular walking reduces venous stasis rather than increasing risk. E. A healed minor skin wound carries no VTE risk.
pearl: Virchow's triad of stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability explains why surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy and oestrogen therapy all increase VTE risk.
thinking: Think of Virchow's triad ↓ Look for stasis, vessel injury or hypercoagulability ↓ Major joint surgery causes vessel injury and hypercoagulability ↓ Bed rest adds stasis ↓ Hip replacement patient is at risk
exam_trap: E, A healed graze on the knee — a wound sounds like tissue injury, but a superficial healed graze does not affect deep venous flow or clotting.
takeaway: Major surgery followed by immobility is a classic VTE risk factor that should prompt thromboprophylaxis.

stem:
A 34-year-old man is reviewed in the anticoagulation clinic after a left femoral vein thrombosis that occurred with no surgery, travel or illness beforehand. His sister had a pulmonary embolism in her twenties and his father had recurrent leg clots.

Which inherited disorder is most likely to explain this family pattern?
why_correct: Factor V Leiden is the commonest inherited thrombophilia in people of European descent. The mutated factor V resists inactivation by activated protein C, so clotting is less well switched off and venous thrombosis is more likely. Unprovoked clots in a young man with several affected first-degree relatives fit this autosomal dominant pattern.
why_wrong: A. Haemophilia B is an X-linked bleeding disorder, not a clotting tendency. B. G6PD deficiency causes episodic haemolysis after oxidant triggers. C. Von Willebrand disease causes mucosal bleeding. D. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolytic anaemia, jaundice and gallstones.
pearl: Factor V Leiden is detected functionally as activated protein C resistance, and heterozygotes have a several-fold increase in venous thrombosis risk.
thinking: Young adult with unprovoked venous clot ↓ Strong family history of VTE ↓ Suggests inherited thrombophilia ↓ Exclude bleeding and haemolytic disorders ↓ Commonest cause is factor V Leiden
exam_trap: C, Von Willebrand disease — it is the commonest inherited coagulation disorder, which tempts recognition, but it causes bleeding rather than thrombosis.
takeaway: Unprovoked VTE with a strong family history should raise the possibility of factor V Leiden.

stem:
A 26-year-old man with newly diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma is being staged in the haematology clinic. He describes soaking his sheets most nights, temperatures above 38 °C with no infection found, and losing more than a tenth of his body weight over four months without trying.

What term is used for this group of features?
why_correct: Unexplained fevers above 38 °C, drenching night sweats and loss of more than 10% of body weight over 6 months are known as B symptoms. They are recorded at staging because their presence is added as the suffix B to the stage and indicates a worse prognosis. He has all three features.
why_wrong: A. Paraneoplastic syndromes are remote effects such as hypercalcaemia or neuropathy, not this staging triad. B. Horner syndrome is ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis from sympathetic chain disruption. C. Cushingoid features result from glucocorticoid excess. D. Tumour lysis causes metabolic disturbance after treatment starts, not weight loss and sweats at diagnosis.
pearl: Generalised itching and alcohol-induced pain in affected nodes are recognised features of Hodgkin lymphoma but are not counted as B symptoms.
thinking: Lymphoma being staged ↓ Fever, drenching sweats, weight loss ↓ These three define B symptoms ↓ Added as suffix B to the stage ↓ Indicate more advanced disease and worse prognosis
exam_trap: A, Paraneoplastic syndrome — systemic features of cancer sound paraneoplastic, but the fever, sweats and weight loss triad has its own staging name in lymphoma.
takeaway: Fever, drenching night sweats and significant weight loss in lymphoma are called B symptoms and affect staging.

stem:
A 41-year-old aid worker sees her GP six weeks after returning from a year in rural West Africa, where she often swam in freshwater lakes. She has vague abdominal pain and an itchy rash. A full blood count shows a raised eosinophil count on two occasions, with normal haemoglobin.

What is the most likely underlying cause?
why_correct: Persistent eosinophilia in a returning traveller should be assumed to be due to a helminth infection until proven otherwise. Tissue-invasive worms such as schistosoma and strongyloides commonly cause eosinophilia, and freshwater exposure in Africa is a classic risk for schistosomiasis. Stool microscopy and serology are appropriate next steps.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency causes a microcytic anaemia, not eosinophilia. B. Coeliac disease causes malabsorption and anaemia but not raised eosinophils. C. Viral gastroenteritis is short-lived and does not cause persistent eosinophilia. E. Thyrotoxicosis is not a recognised cause of marked eosinophilia.
pearl: Strongyloides can persist for decades through autoinfection and may cause fatal hyperinfection if the person is given corticosteroids, so screen at-risk travellers before immunosuppression.
thinking: Returned from the tropics ↓ Freshwater exposure ↓ Persistent eosinophilia with abdominal symptoms ↓ Tissue-invasive helminths are the commonest cause ↓ Send stool and serology for parasites
exam_trap: C, Viral gastroenteritis — abdominal symptoms after travel make an infective gut cause tempting, but viruses do not cause persistent eosinophilia.
takeaway: Persistent eosinophilia after tropical travel suggests a parasitic worm infection.

stem:
A 52-year-old man has a raised ALT on three blood tests over a year, ordered at his annual diabetes review. He drinks within recommended limits and has no features of fatty liver on ultrasound. He mentions that he injected heroin with friends in his twenties.

Which infection is most important to test for?
why_correct: Past injecting drug use is the main risk factor for hepatitis C in the UK, because the virus spreads efficiently through shared needles and equipment. Most infections become chronic and are often silent, presenting only with persistently raised transaminases. He should be offered an antibody test followed by HCV RNA if positive, since curative antiviral treatment is available.
why_wrong: B. Hepatitis A spreads faeco-orally and causes only an acute self-limiting illness. C. Cytomegalovirus can cause a transient hepatitis but is not linked to injecting or chronic enzyme rise. D. Norovirus causes acute vomiting and diarrhoea, not liver disease. E. Hepatitis E is mainly food-borne and rarely chronic outside immunosuppression.
pearl: Many people with chronic hepatitis C have no symptoms for decades, so anyone who has ever injected drugs should be offered testing even if it was long ago.
thinking: Persistently raised liver enzymes ↓ Alcohol and fatty liver less likely ↓ History of injecting drug use ↓ Blood-borne virus with chronic infection ↓ Test for hepatitis C
exam_trap: E, Hepatitis E virus — it is a common cause of hepatitis in the UK, but it is food-borne and usually acute, with no link to shared needles.
takeaway: Persistently abnormal liver tests in someone who has injected drugs should prompt hepatitis C testing.

stem:
A 33-year-old man phones his GP practice in England for advice from his hotel in rural Indonesia. An hour ago a monkey jumped onto him at a temple and bit his forearm, drawing blood. He had no rabies vaccines before travelling and feels well.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Wash the bite thoroughly with soap and water and seek medical care urgently for rabies post-exposure treatment
options.B: Watch for tingling at the bite site and seek help only if it develops
options.C: Start the co-amoxiclav from his travel kit, which will prevent rabies
options.D: Book a rabies vaccine course with his GP once he is home
options.E: Wait to see whether the monkey becomes unwell before acting

correct_answer: A. Wash the bite thoroughly with soap and water and seek medical care urgently for rabies post-exposure treatment
why_correct: Any bite from a mammal in a rabies-endemic country is a potential rabies exposure, and the disease is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. Immediate thorough washing for several minutes reduces viral load, and he needs urgent local medical assessment for vaccine and, as he is unvaccinated with a bleeding bite, rabies immunoglobulin. UKHSA can advise on risk and prophylaxis after return.
why_wrong: B. Waiting for symptoms is unsafe because clinical rabies is essentially untreatable. C. Antibiotics may treat bacterial wound infection but have no effect on the rabies virus. D. Delaying until return loses critical time and routine vaccination is not post-exposure treatment. E. A monkey cannot be observed reliably, and waiting delays prophylaxis.
pearl: Wild or stray monkeys and bats carry rabies risk as well as dogs, and observation of the animal for 10 days is only meaningful for domestic dogs, cats and ferrets.
thinking: Mammal bite in rabies-endemic area ↓ Skin broken and bleeding ↓ Not previously vaccinated ↓ Wash wound thoroughly now ↓ Urgent post-exposure vaccine with immunoglobulin
exam_trap: D, Book a rabies vaccine course with his GP once he is home — it acknowledges the need for vaccine, but post-exposure prophylaxis is time-critical and should start as soon as possible.
takeaway: After a potential rabies exposure abroad, wash the wound and get urgent post-exposure prophylaxis without waiting.
notes: Reviewer fix: Stem: patient in Indonesia cannot call NHS 111 (UK-only); changed to phoning his GP practice in England.

stem:
A 45-year-old woman is admitted to the infectious diseases unit with agitation and confusion. Two months earlier she was nipped on the ankle by a stray dog in northern India and did not seek treatment. The illness began with a low-grade temperature and burning pain around the healed bite. She now has violent throat spasms when offered a drink and becomes distressed when a fan blows air on her face.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rabies classically begins with fever and paraesthesia or pain at the healed bite site, then progresses to encephalitis. Hydrophobia, triggered by pharyngeal spasm on attempting to drink, and aerophobia from a draught of air are pathognomonic of furious rabies. An untreated dog bite in an endemic country weeks to months earlier fits the incubation period.
why_wrong: A. Tetanus causes trismus, rigidity and spasms with a clear sensorium, not hydrophobia or confusion. C. Japanese encephalitis is mosquito-borne and lacks bite-site symptoms and hydrophobia. D. Cerebral malaria causes fever and reduced consciousness but not pharyngeal spasm on drinking. E. Herpes simplex encephalitis causes confusion and fever but not hydrophobia or aerophobia.
pearl: Once symptoms of rabies appear, death is almost certain, so care focuses on palliation and protection of staff, while contacts may need assessment for prophylaxis.
thinking: Untreated dog bite in an endemic country ↓ Incubation of weeks to months ↓ Fever with pain at old bite site ↓ Hydrophobia and aerophobia ↓ Rabies encephalitis
exam_trap: A, Tetanus — it follows a wound and causes muscle spasm, but patients remain alert and do not have spasm triggered by water or air.
takeaway: Hydrophobia and aerophobia after an animal bite abroad are hallmarks of rabies.

presentation: Rabies risk after dog bite abroad
stem:
A 61-year-old retired teacher returns from a trip to Morocco and attends a walk-in centre. Four days ago a street dog bit her calf as she walked through a market. The wound was rinsed but she saw no doctor, and the owner of the dog could not be found. Her tetanus immunisations are complete.

Which infection is the most urgent concern?
why_correct: Morocco is a rabies-endemic country, and a bite from a stray dog whose health cannot be checked is a significant potential exposure. Because rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms develop but is preventable with timely post-exposure prophylaxis, it is the most urgent concern even several days later. She should be discussed with the UKHSA rabies service and started on prophylaxis as advised.
why_wrong: A. Leptospirosis is acquired from water contaminated with animal urine, not dog bites. C. Malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes. D. Measles is spread by respiratory droplets. E. Tetanus should always be considered after a wound, but her immunisations are complete and it does not replace rabies assessment.
pearl: Post-exposure prophylaxis is still worthwhile days or even weeks after an exposure, because the rabies incubation period is usually 1 to 3 months.
thinking: Dog bite in a rabies-endemic country ↓ Animal unknown and cannot be observed ↓ Rabies is fatal once symptomatic ↓ Still within the window for prophylaxis ↓ Urgent rabies risk assessment
exam_trap: E, Tetanus — it is routinely considered after any bite, but her vaccinations are complete and the life-threatening, time-critical risk here is rabies.
takeaway: A dog bite in a rabies-endemic country needs urgent rabies risk assessment even if days have passed.

stem:
A 38-year-old postman is seen at a minor injuries unit after a neighbour's pet dog bit his hand through his glove, leaving several soil-contaminated puncture wounds. He has never left the UK and the dog is well and vaccinated. He cannot remember any vaccinations since school.

Which vaccine-preventable infection must be specifically addressed?
why_correct: Bites that break the skin are tetanus-prone wounds, especially when contaminated with soil. His immunisation history is uncertain, so he needs a tetanus vaccine booster and, depending on the risk assessment, human tetanus immunoglobulin, following UKHSA Green Book guidance. Wound cleaning and antibiotic prophylaxis are also considered.
why_wrong: A. A bite from a well, vaccinated UK pet dog carries no realistic rabies risk. B. Hepatitis A is spread by the faeco-oral route, not bites. C. Measles is spread by airborne droplets. E. Rubella is spread by respiratory droplets.
pearl: A tetanus-prone wound in someone whose immunisation status is unknown or incomplete needs an immediate reinforcing dose of tetanus vaccine, with human tetanus immunoglobulin given according to the Green Book wound-risk assessment.
thinking: Skin broken by a dog bite ↓ Wound contaminated with soil ↓ Tetanus history uncertain ↓ No overseas or rabies risk ↓ Address tetanus immunisation
exam_trap: A, Rabies — dog bites instantly bring rabies to mind, but a vaccinated UK pet with no travel link poses no real risk, whereas tetanus cover is genuinely uncertain.
takeaway: Every bite that breaks the skin needs the patient's tetanus status checked and treated if incomplete.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl reworded to Green Book: immediate reinforcing tetanus dose for tetanus-prone wound with unknown status, HTIG per wound-risk assessment (was over-simplified 'only if high risk').

stem:
An 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his father after being bitten on the forearm by a friend's dog an hour ago. The wound is a small tear that is no longer bleeding, and his father asks whether they can simply go home.

What should the initial management include?

options.A: Close the wound tightly with sutures and discharge
options.B: Give oral antibiotics and discharge without examining the wound
options.C: Reassure and discharge without assessment because the bleeding has stopped
options.D: Record only the wound size, as the animal's details are not relevant
options.E: Clean and assess the wound, judge infection risk and check tetanus immunisation

correct_answer: E. Clean and assess the wound, judge infection risk and check tetanus immunisation
why_correct: Every animal bite needs proper assessment even when small. The wound should be irrigated and examined for depth and damage to deeper structures, the infection risk judged from the site, animal and delay, and tetanus immunisation status checked. The animal and circumstances are documented as they affect decisions on antibiotics and rabies risk.
why_wrong: A. Primary closure of bites is not routine and tight suturing traps bacteria. B. Antibiotic decisions depend on assessing the wound first. C. Small bites can still become infected or involve deeper tissues. D. The type of animal and its circumstances guide antibiotic and rabies decisions.
pearl: NICE advises prophylactic co-amoxiclav for cat bites that break the skin and for dog bites that break the skin and draw blood; for a dog bite that breaks the skin without drawing blood it is considered if the bite is to a high-risk area such as the hand, foot or face, or the person is at high risk of serious infection.
thinking: Animal bite in a child ↓ Small wound does not mean low risk ↓ Irrigate and examine depth ↓ Judge infection risk and need for antibiotics ↓ Check tetanus status and document the animal
exam_trap: B, Give oral antibiotics and discharge without examining the wound — antibiotics are often given after bites, but prescribing without assessing the wound can miss deep injury and inappropriate use adds harm.
takeaway: All animal bites need cleaning, assessment of infection risk and a tetanus check.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl corrected to NICE NG184: co-amoxiclav for cat bites breaking skin and dog bites breaking skin and drawing blood; considered for non-bleeding dog bites only in high-risk sites/people.

stem:
A 76-year-old man in a care home was started on amoxicillin by the out-of-hours GP for a community-acquired pneumonia. At review on day 3 his fever has settled, he is eating again and his breathing is back to normal. The care home manager asks whether the antibiotic should be changed.

What is the most appropriate prescribing approach?

options.A: Stop the antibiotic today because he has recovered
options.B: Extend the course to 3 weeks to prevent relapse
options.C: Double the dose to secure the response
options.D: Add clarithromycin to protect against resistance
options.E: Confirm the diagnosis and complete the recommended course length, then stop

correct_answer: E. Confirm the diagnosis and complete the recommended course length, then stop
why_correct: Antimicrobial stewardship means reviewing every antibiotic prescription against the diagnosis and clinical response. For low-severity community-acquired pneumonia NICE recommends a 5-day course, so he should complete the recommended duration and then stop. Improvement does not justify stopping early, extending, escalating or adding agents.
why_wrong: A. Improvement alone does not mean the infection is fully treated; course length depends on the diagnosis. B. Unnecessarily long courses increase side effects, C. difficile risk and resistance. C. Increasing the dose has no benefit when he is responding. D. Adding a second antibiotic without indication is poor stewardship.
pearl: Shorter antibiotic courses are now recommended for many common infections, so prescriptions should state the duration and be reviewed rather than continued by default.
thinking: Antibiotic started for a defined infection ↓ Patient responding well ↓ Review against diagnosis and guidance ↓ No need to escalate or extend ↓ Complete recommended duration then stop
exam_trap: A, Stop the antibiotic today because he has recovered — it sounds like good stewardship, but stopping depends on the recommended course for the diagnosis, not on feeling better.
takeaway: Review antibiotics against the diagnosis and give the recommended duration, no longer and no shorter.

stem:
A 63-year-old woman visits her GP the morning after her cat bit the base of her thumb while she was giving it a tablet. There are two tiny puncture marks that have already closed, and the hand is not yet red or swollen. She thinks it does not need any treatment because the marks are so small.

What is the most important reason to take this injury seriously?

options.A: Cat bites usually transmit rabies in the UK
options.B: Cat bites are only significant if they bleed heavily
options.C: Small wounds that close quickly cannot become infected
options.D: Tetanus is the only risk that needs to be checked
options.E: Cat teeth inject bacteria deep into tissue, so hand bites carry a high infection risk

correct_answer: E. Cat teeth inject bacteria deep into tissue, so hand bites carry a high infection risk
why_correct: Cat teeth are thin and sharp, so they carry bacteria such as Pasteurella multocida deep into tissues and the puncture seals over, creating ideal conditions for infection. Bites to the hand can rapidly lead to cellulitis, tenosynovitis or septic arthritis. NICE advises prophylactic antibiotics for cat bites that have broken the skin.
why_wrong: A. Domestic cats in the UK are not a rabies source. B. Deep punctures are high risk regardless of how much they bleed. C. A wound that seals over traps bacteria and makes infection more likely. D. Tetanus status matters but bacterial infection is the main risk.
pearl: Pasteurella multocida infection after a cat bite can cause rapidly spreading cellulitis within 24 hours, and co-amoxiclav is the usual first-line choice.
thinking: Cat bite ↓ Narrow deep puncture that seals over ↓ Bacteria inoculated into deep tissue ↓ Hand involvement risks tendon and joint infection ↓ Treat as high risk and give prophylactic antibiotics
exam_trap: C, Small wounds that close quickly cannot become infected — the tiny closed marks look reassuring, but sealed punctures are exactly what makes cat bites so prone to infection.
takeaway: Cat bites, especially to the hand, carry a high infection risk despite small-looking wounds.

stem:
A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department on a Sunday morning with a small cut over the knuckle of his right middle finger. He admits he hit someone in the face outside a nightclub the night before. The finger is mildly swollen and painful to bend.

Which injury does this most likely represent?

options.A: Simple abrasion from a rough surface
options.B: Boxer's fracture of the fifth metacarpal
options.E: Human tooth injury to the hand with risk of joint and tendon infection

correct_answer: E. Human tooth injury to the hand with risk of joint and tendon infection
why_correct: A wound over a knuckle after punching someone in the mouth is a fight bite until proven otherwise. The tooth can penetrate the extensor tendon and metacarpophalangeal joint capsule when the fist is clenched, inoculating oral bacteria deep into the joint. These injuries need exploration, irrigation, X-ray, antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav and often hand surgery review.
why_wrong: A. Labelling it a simple abrasion misses deep contamination by oral flora. B. A boxer's fracture involves the fifth metacarpal neck and causes deformity, and the skin wound here is over the middle knuckle. C. A blister does not explain a penetrating wound after a punch. D. The skin is broken, so this is not a closed bruise.
pearl: When the fist is unclenched the tendon wound moves away from the skin wound, so the depth of a fight bite is often underestimated on examination.
thinking: Punched someone in the face ↓ Wound over the knuckle ↓ Tooth may enter joint and tendon sheath ↓ Oral bacteria inoculated deeply ↓ Treat as a high-risk human bite
exam_trap: B, Boxer's fracture of the fifth metacarpal — a punch injury immediately suggests a fracture, but a skin wound over the knuckle after hitting a face points to a contaminated human bite.
takeaway: A knuckle wound after punching someone in the mouth is a high-risk human bite.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman sees her GP with a widespread seborrhoeic dermatitis-like rash, recurrent oral thrush and a recent episode of shingles. She has no known risk factors and is worried about what is causing these problems. The GP thinks HIV infection is possible.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Test only if she reports a high-risk sexual history
options.B: Refer for formal pre-test counselling at a specialist clinic first
options.C: Explain why testing is advised, obtain her verbal consent and offer an HIV test
options.D: Add HIV to her blood tests without telling her to avoid alarming her
options.E: Test and, if positive, inform her employer for occupational health purposes

correct_answer: C. Explain why testing is advised, obtain her verbal consent and offer an HIV test
why_correct: HIV testing should be offered whenever the clinical picture includes an indicator condition, regardless of perceived risk group, as advised by NICE NG60 and BHIVA. Oral candidiasis, shingles and seborrhoeic dermatitis are indicator conditions. Any clinician can offer the test after a brief explanation and verbal consent, and the result is kept confidential.
why_wrong: A. Restricting tests to perceived risk groups misses many diagnoses. B. Lengthy specialist pre-test counselling is no longer required. D. Testing without her knowledge breaches consent. E. Disclosure to an employer breaches confidentiality.
pearl: Late HIV diagnosis is a major cause of avoidable illness and death in the UK, so testing should be normalised and offered whenever an indicator condition is present.
thinking: Several HIV indicator conditions ↓ HIV is in the differential ↓ Risk group is irrelevant ↓ Brief explanation and verbal consent ↓ Offer test and keep result confidential
exam_trap: B, Refer for formal pre-test counselling at a specialist clinic first — it seems thorough, but extended counselling is not required and the delay risks missing a diagnosis.
takeaway: When HIV is clinically possible, offer a test with simple verbal consent and confidentiality.

stem: At a drug and alcohol service, a 44-year-old woman who injected heroin in her twenties asks to be checked for blood-borne infections. She has never been tested before and is currently well. Her keyworker asks which blood test should be sent first to find out whether she has ever been infected with hepatitis C.
why_correct: Antibody testing for hepatitis C is the standard first-line screen for people at risk, such as those with a history of injecting drug use. A positive antibody shows exposure at some point but cannot distinguish cleared from ongoing infection. A reactive result is therefore followed by HCV RNA (or core antigen) testing, ideally reflexively on the same sample, to confirm current infection.
why_wrong: B. Hepatitis B core antibody indicates past hepatitis B exposure, not hepatitis C. C. Liver function tests may be normal in chronic hepatitis C and are not a screening test. D. HIV RNA tests for HIV infection, not hepatitis C. E. Hepatitis A IgM detects recent hepatitis A infection only.
pearl: About a quarter of people infected with hepatitis C clear the virus spontaneously, so they remain antibody positive but RNA negative.
thinking: History of injecting drug use ↓ Recognised risk group for hepatitis C ↓ Screening aims to detect any past exposure ↓ HCV antibody is the initial test ↓ Confirm current infection with HCV RNA if reactive
exam_trap: C, Liver function tests — raised transaminases feel like a natural first check for hepatitis, but many people with chronic hepatitis C have normal liver enzymes.
takeaway: Screen for hepatitis C with an antibody test, then confirm active infection with HCV RNA.

stem:
A 52-year-old man in prison has a positive hepatitis C RNA test during a routine health check. He tells the prison nurse that a relative was told years ago that nothing could be done for the infection, and he assumes the same applies to him.

What is the most accurate advice?

options.A: Oral direct-acting antiviral treatment cures most people with chronic hepatitis C
options.B: A course of broad-spectrum antibiotics will clear the virus
options.C: Vaccination now will clear the existing infection
options.D: No treatment is needed because hepatitis C does not cause long-term liver damage
options.E: Only a liver transplant can remove the virus

correct_answer: A. Oral direct-acting antiviral treatment cures most people with chronic hepatitis C
why_correct: Chronic hepatitis C is now curable in most people with a short course of oral direct-acting antivirals, usually taken for 8 to 12 weeks. Cure is defined as a sustained virological response, with no detectable RNA after treatment. He should be referred to the hepatitis C treatment network, and care in prison does not prevent this.
why_wrong: B. Antibiotics have no activity against viruses. C. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C, and vaccines do not treat established infection. D. Chronic hepatitis C can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. E. Transplant is reserved for end-stage liver disease or liver cancer, and antivirals clear the virus without it.
pearl: Older interferon-based regimens were poorly tolerated and less effective, which is why many patients still believe hepatitis C cannot be treated.
thinking: Positive HCV RNA means current infection ↓ Patient believes it is untreatable ↓ Direct-acting antivirals are oral and short-course ↓ Most people achieve cure ↓ Refer for antiviral treatment
exam_trap: E, Only a liver transplant can remove the virus — it sounds plausible for a serious liver infection, but transplant treats end-stage liver failure, not the virus itself.
takeaway: Most people with chronic hepatitis C can be cured with oral direct-acting antivirals.

stem:
A newly qualified healthcare assistant attends occupational health to start her hepatitis B vaccine course. She asks whether she can also be vaccinated against hepatitis C at the same appointment, since she will be handling blood samples.

What is the correct response?

options.A: Yes, a hepatitis C vaccine is given with the hepatitis B course
options.B: No, there is no licensed vaccine that prevents hepatitis C
options.C: Yes, but only after checking hepatitis C antibody levels
options.D: Her MMR vaccination will already protect her against hepatitis C
