options.E: She does not need protection because hepatitis C is spread only by food

correct_answer: B. No, there is no licensed vaccine that prevents hepatitis C
why_correct: No vaccine against hepatitis C is licensed or routinely available. Protection for healthcare workers relies on standard infection-control precautions, safe sharps handling and prompt reporting and follow-up of any exposure. The hepatitis B vaccine does not protect against hepatitis C.
why_wrong: A. No combined or separate hepatitis C vaccine exists. C. Antibody levels are irrelevant as there is no vaccine to give. D. MMR protects against measles, mumps and rubella only. E. Hepatitis C is blood-borne, so her role does carry some risk.
pearl: Hepatitis A and B have effective vaccines, whereas hepatitis C has none, partly because of its high genetic variability.
thinking: Healthcare worker asks about hepatitis C vaccine ↓ Hepatitis B vaccine exists, hepatitis C does not ↓ Prevention relies on safe practice ↓ Report and follow up any sharps injury
exam_trap: A, Yes, a hepatitis C vaccine is given with the hepatitis B course — combined hepatitis A and B vaccines exist, which makes a hepatitis C product seem believable.
takeaway: There is no vaccine against hepatitis C; prevention relies on avoiding blood exposure.

stem:
A 19-year-old man calls NHS 111, worried after learning that a friend he lives with has HIV. Over the past month they have shared meals, a bathroom and on one occasion a needle and syringe when injecting steroids at the gym.

Which of these exposures carries a real risk of HIV transmission?

options.A: Eating from the same plates and cutlery
options.E: Being coughed on while sitting together

correct_answer: C. Sharing the needle and syringe
why_correct: HIV is transmitted through blood, semen, vaginal fluids and breast milk. Sharing injecting equipment introduces infected blood directly into the bloodstream and is a well-recognised route of transmission. He should be offered HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C testing and advice on needle exchange services.
why_wrong: A. Saliva and shared crockery do not transmit HIV. B. HIV does not survive or spread via toilet seats. D. Intact skin contact does not transmit HIV. E. HIV is not spread by respiratory droplets.
pearl: If an exposure is recent (within 72 hours), post-exposure prophylaxis may be considered, so the timing of the exposure should always be asked about.
thinking: Friend has HIV ↓ List the types of contact ↓ HIV needs blood or sexual fluids ↓ Shared needle gives direct blood exposure ↓ Offer blood-borne virus testing
exam_trap: E, Being coughed on while sitting together — many people assume close-range coughing spreads any infection, but HIV is not airborne.
takeaway: Shared injecting equipment is a true HIV risk; everyday social contact is not.

stem:
A 30-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic after condomless sex with a new partner. While his screening samples are taken, he asks which of the infections on the list he could protect himself against in future by having a vaccine, and he means the one that is passed on through blood as well as through sex.

Which infection is it?
why_correct: Hepatitis B is spread by blood, sexual contact and from mother to baby, and an effective vaccine is available. Sexual health clinics offer hepatitis B vaccination to people at increased risk. None of the other listed infections has a routinely available preventive vaccine.
why_wrong: A. Chlamydia is sexually transmitted but not blood-borne, and there is no vaccine. C. Syphilis has no vaccine. D. Hepatitis C is blood-borne but has no vaccine. E. HIV has no vaccine, although pre-exposure prophylaxis can prevent infection.
pearl: Hepatitis B vaccine is part of the routine UK infant schedule within the 6-in-1 vaccine.
thinking: Infection spread by blood and sex ↓ Must also be vaccine-preventable ↓ Hepatitis C and HIV have no vaccine ↓ Hepatitis B fits both features
exam_trap: E, HIV — it is the classic blood and sexually transmitted virus, and PrEP is easily confused with a vaccine, but no HIV vaccine exists.
takeaway: Hepatitis B is the vaccine-preventable blood-borne and sexually transmitted virus.
notes: Reviewer fix: Gonorrhoea distractor replaced with chlamydia (UK now offers 4CMenB to prevent gonorrhoea, making 'no vaccine' misleading); stem reworded to remove the illogical 'prevented by a vaccine he could still have now'.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman sees her GP two weeks after returning from backpacking in South Asia, where she often drank from street stalls. She has gradually worsening lower abdominal cramps and loose stools streaked with blood and mucus. Stool microscopy reveals a parasite.

Which protozoan best explains her illness?
why_correct: Entamoeba histolytica invades the colonic mucosa, producing amoebic dysentery with gradual-onset abdominal pain and bloody, mucoid diarrhoea. It is acquired through faecally contaminated food or water, typically in travellers to areas with poor sanitation. It can also spread to cause an amoebic liver abscess.
why_wrong: B. Giardia causes non-bloody, greasy diarrhoea with bloating and malabsorption. C. Cryptosporidium causes watery, non-bloody diarrhoea. D. Toxoplasma causes a glandular-fever-like illness or congenital and CNS disease, not dysentery. E. Plasmodium vivax causes malaria, not bloody diarrhoea.
pearl: Treatment of invasive amoebiasis is metronidazole followed by a luminal agent such as diloxanide furoate to eradicate cysts.
thinking: Recent travel with contaminated water ↓ Bloody diarrhoea with mucus ↓ Parasite on stool microscopy ↓ Invasive colonic protozoan ↓ Entamoeba histolytica
exam_trap: B, Giardia intestinalis — it is the protozoan most associated with travel and contaminated water, but it does not invade the mucosa and so the stool is not bloody.
takeaway: A protozoal cause of bloody diarrhoea in a traveller is Entamoeba histolytica.

stem:
Three days after a summer barbecue where the chicken was pink in the middle, a 45-year-old man attends the urgent treatment centre. He has a temperature, crampy abdominal pain and diarrhoea that started watery and now contains blood.

Which organism is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Campylobacter is the commonest bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in the UK and is strongly linked to undercooked poultry. It typically causes fever and cramping abdominal pain with diarrhoea that may become bloody after a short incubation period. Most cases settle without antibiotics.
why_wrong: A. Cholera causes profuse rice-water diarrhoea without blood. B. Clostridium tetani causes tetanus with muscle spasm, not diarrhoea. C. Giardia gives prolonged non-bloody diarrhoea with bloating. E. Treponema pallidum causes syphilis.
pearl: Campylobacter infection is the commonest recognised trigger of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
thinking: Undercooked chicken ↓ Short incubation of a few days ↓ Fever and cramps ↓ Diarrhoea becoming bloody ↓ Campylobacter
exam_trap: C, Giardia intestinalis — it is a familiar cause of diarrhoea, but it gives prolonged non-bloody stools and is linked to water rather than poultry.
takeaway: Bloody diarrhoea with fever after undercooked poultry suggests Campylobacter.

stem:
Several toddlers at the same nursery have been unwell this week. A 4-year-old girl from that group is brought to the GP by her father: she is hot, keeps clutching her tummy and strains on the potty, producing only a little each time, streaked red and slimy.

Which bacterium most likely explains her illness?
why_correct: Shigella causes bacillary dysentery with fever, cramping pain, tenesmus and frequent small-volume stools containing blood and mucus. It has a very low infective dose, so it spreads easily from person to person in nurseries and households. Shigella sonnei is the commonest species in the UK, and shigellosis is a notifiable disease.
why_wrong: A. Bacillus cereus causes short-lived vomiting or watery diarrhoea from toxins, not dysentery. B. Cholera causes large-volume watery diarrhoea. D. Cryptosporidium causes watery diarrhoea. E. Giardia causes non-bloody diarrhoea with malabsorption.
pearl: Children with shigellosis should be excluded from nursery until 48 hours after their last episode of diarrhoea, and some cases need microbiological clearance.
thinking: Outbreak in a nursery ↓ Fever and tenesmus ↓ Small frequent stools with blood and mucus ↓ Low infective dose bacterium ↓ Shigella
exam_trap: D, Cryptosporidium parvum — it is a well-known cause of outbreaks among young children, but it produces watery rather than bloody stools.
takeaway: Fever with small, frequent bloody mucoid stools is the classic picture of Shigella dysentery.

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is admitted from the children's ward assessment unit with bloody diarrhoea that began after a family meal of homemade burgers. Stool testing confirms E. coli O157, a Shiga toxin-producing strain. His parents ask which serious complication the team will be monitoring for over the next week.

Which is it?
why_correct: Shiga toxin damages endothelium, particularly in the kidney, causing haemolytic uraemic syndrome in a proportion of infected children. It usually develops around a week after the diarrhoea starts. Children are therefore monitored with blood counts, renal function and urine output, and antibiotics and antimotility drugs are avoided.
why_wrong: A. Reactive arthritis follows infections such as Salmonella, Shigella and Campylobacter and is not the key STEC complication. B. Toxic shock syndrome is caused by staphylococcal or streptococcal toxins. C. Guillain-Barré syndrome is classically linked to Campylobacter. E. Endocarditis is not a complication of STEC enteritis.
pearl: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome, usually triggered by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, is the commonest cause of acute kidney injury in UK children.
thinking: Bloody diarrhoea after undercooked beef ↓ STEC O157 confirmed ↓ Shiga toxin injures renal endothelium ↓ Risk peaks about a week in ↓ Monitor for haemolytic uraemic syndrome
exam_trap: C, Guillain-Barré syndrome — it is a well-known complication of bacterial gastroenteritis, but it is linked with Campylobacter rather than STEC.
takeaway: The key complication to watch for after STEC infection is haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl corrected: HUS (usually from STEC) is the commonest cause of AKI in UK children, not STEC itself.
